title: The LORD Sits Enthroned: Thanks for Justice Done
summary: David gives thanks with his whole heart for the LORD's wonders, especially his justice: God has judged the nations, upheld the psalmist's cause, and proved a stronghold for the oppressed. The psalm then turns to prayer, asking for mercy in present trouble and for God to rise up and remind the nations that they are only human. The needy, it promises, will not be forgotten forever.
story: Psalm 8 praised God's majestic name in all the earth; Psalm 9 praises the same God as king and judge over the nations. The small, personal troubles of the earlier laments are now set on a world stage. The God who hears the cry of one afflicted person also sits enthroned over empires. Psalm 9 is also the first half of a larger poem that continues in Psalm 10, and the two should be read together. Psalm 9 leans toward thanksgiving and confidence; Psalm 10 leans toward lament and the question of why God seems far away. Together they hold praise and complaint side by side, which is how the Psalter as a whole speaks.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and names a tune, “The Death of the Son”, whose meaning is unknown. Some ancient interpreters connected the phrase with the death of Goliath or of one of David's sons, but those are guesses. The psalm's references to nations being rebuked and cities uprooted fit David's wars with neighboring peoples described in 2 Samuel 8, though nothing in the text requires a specific campaign. Scholars who date the headings later often read the psalm as a liturgical song of the Jerusalem temple, used whenever Israel recalled God's past victories and asked for help against present oppressors.

Psalms 9 and 10 share an incomplete acrostic, and Psalm 10 lacks a heading, which is unusual in the first book of the Psalter. The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) and the Latin Vulgate treat them as one psalm. Because of that, the traditional numbering of the Psalms in Greek and Latin Bibles runs one number behind the Hebrew numbering for most of the book, which is why older Catholic and Orthodox references can differ from Protestant ones.
cultural:
An acrostic is a poem in which each section begins with the next letter of the alphabet, a form used in several psalms (25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119, 145) and in Lamentations 1 to 4. It may have aided memory and conveyed completeness, praise from A to Z. In Psalms 9 and 10 the pattern is present but broken in places, and scholars debate whether the text was damaged in transmission or the poet deliberately let the pattern falter in the stretches of complaint.

The psalm draws on Israel's ideas of kingship and justice. A king sat on a throne to hear cases, and his first duty was to protect the weak: the poor, the widow, the orphan, the stranger. Verse 12 calls God “the Avenger of bloodshed” (literally the one who seeks out blood), an image that recalls the avenger of blood in Israel's law, the relative responsible for pursuing justice when a family member was killed (Numbers 35:19). City gates were the place of public life and legal hearings; the “gates of death” in verse 13 and the “gates of Daughter Zion” in verse 14 set two assemblies side by side. “Daughter Zion” is a poetic personification of Jerusalem and its people. Higgaion, at verse 16, is another musical or liturgical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps a quiet interlude or a call to meditate.
literary: The psalm moves from thanksgiving (verses 1 and 2), through a report of God's past victories and his enthronement as judge (verses 3 to 12), to prayer for help in present trouble (verses 13 and 14), confidence that the wicked will fall into their own traps (verses 15 to 18), and a closing call for God to rise up (verses 19 and 20). Verses 7 and 8 are its center: the LORD abides forever, enthroned for judgment. Key words repeat: judge and judgment, throne, nations, forget and remember. The nations who forget God (verse 17) are set against the God who does not forget the needy (verse 18), a contrast that Psalm 10 will test hard. The final line, “let the nations know they are but men”, echoes the humility of Psalm 8.

outline.t: The LORD enthroned as judge and refuge
A plea for mercy from the gates of death
The wicked caught; the needy not forgotten
Rise up, O LORD: the nations are only human

doctrines.note: The LORD “abides forever” and has “established His throne for judgment”. His rule is not limited to Israel; he judges the world and the nations with equity.
God's judgment in this psalm is protection for the oppressed as much as punishment for the wicked. The verdict against the nations is also a warning against pride: they are only human.
Verse 18 is a promise to the poor: their hope will not be forever dashed. The psalm grounds that hope in God's past acts and in his unchanging throne.

words.note: Misgav, stronghold or high refuge. It means a secure height, a fortified place out of an enemy's reach. Verse 9 uses it twice in parallel lines, first for the oppressed and then for times of trouble. The image is military and physical: God is the place you can run to and not be reached.

Mishpat, justice. It can mean a single legal verdict, a person's rightful claim, or the whole order of fair dealing in a community. Verse 16 says the LORD is known by the justice he brings. In the Old Testament, justice is one of the main ways God reveals who he is.

Ani, afflicted or poor. The word describes people who are low, oppressed, and without power to defend themselves. The Psalms repeatedly say that God hears their cry (verse 12) and remembers them (verse 18). It is also a word the psalmist uses of himself, and it came to describe the humble faithful in Israel.

christ: Psalm 9 celebrates God as the king who judges the world with justice and protects the lowly. The New Testament proclaims that God has appointed Jesus to judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31) and pictures the Son of Man seated on his throne with the nations gathered before him (Matthew 25:31-32). Jesus also takes up the psalm's concern for the afflicted: he announces good news to the poor (Luke 4:18) and says that what is done to the least of his brothers is done to him. These are thematic connections: Psalm 9 does not predict Christ directly, but it describes the kind of king and judge he is revealed to be.

hard.q: Does the psalm celebrate the destruction of whole nations?
hard.a: Verses 5, 6, 15, and 17 speak of nations destroyed, cities uprooted, and the wicked returning to Sheol, and modern readers rightly feel the weight of that. Several things help. The psalm speaks in the language of ancient warfare and of a king defending a threatened people, not of conquest for its own sake; the nations in view are those who oppress, forget God, and ensnare others. The judgment the psalm asks for is God's, not the psalmist's, and it is aimed at humbling pride (verse 20) as much as at destruction. Readers differ on how to relate such language to Jesus' command to love enemies. Some stress that the psalm is a prayer for justice, which Christians still pray; others stress that the New Testament redirects the conflict toward spiritual powers and final judgment rather than earthly wars.

questions: Verse 10 says that those who know God's name trust him. What have you come to know about God that makes trust possible for you?
The psalm insists that God does not forget the needy. Who are the needy and oppressed around you, and how might you share God's attention to them?
Verse 20 asks that the nations know they are only human. Where do individuals, institutions, or nations today forget that they are only human?
